About the Conference

Two days at the edge
of classroom & forest.

Field Notes Live brings together the people who teach, guide, and protect the outdoors — to share what's working, confront what's changing, and leave with tools they can use on Monday morning.

Day One: Field & Workshop

Hands-on sessions outdoors and in. Facilitated workshops, field practicum sessions, and peer-learning labs led by practitioners you trust.

Day Two: Talks & Roundtables

Keynotes and peer roundtables on climate-responsive education, inclusive programming, risk management, and community partnerships.

A Connected Community

Meet park rangers from the Blue Ridge, youth leaders from urban programs, trail stewards, and university researchers — all in one place.

Program Preview

Two days, fully packed.

Day one lives outside — workshops, field sessions, and hands-on learning in the river corridor. Day two moves inside for keynotes, peer roundtables, and sponsor demos.

Featured Speakers

Practitioners with
dirt on their boots.

Every speaker was invited because they work in the field — not just study it. Expect real stories, practical tools, and honest conversation about what's getting harder.

Maya Torres
Keynote Speaker
Director of Interpretation · Blue Ridge Conservancy
"Reading the Land: Integrating Climate Signals into Trail Interpretation"

Maya has spent 15 years training naturalists to read landscape as living data. Her workshops blend phenology, storytelling, and Indigenous ecological knowledge.

Ben Okafor
Session Speaker
Risk Management Specialist · Youth Outdoor Education Network
"Risk-Aware, Not Risk-Averse: Dynamic Safety Planning for Youth Programs"

Ben has developed risk frameworks used by over 400 youth programs nationwide. He argues that overcautious policies are their own kind of harm.

Lila Chen
Session Speaker
Program Director · Accessible Trails Alliance
"No One Left on the Trailhead: Building Truly Inclusive Outdoor Classrooms"

Lila designs programs that center participants who have historically been excluded from outdoor education — urban youth, people with disabilities, and first-generation hikers.
